rv.q: Ostermeier blows the themes of the play up in the most thrilling way.
It is an urgent but tendentious rendering of an ambivalent play.
A play for today, on paper, but the concept could use a digital-era upgrade, and a shot more vigour, to set the world on fire.
But it feels like an elaborate exercise in preaching to the converted.
We do not need to pay West End prices to be beaten around the head like this.
Explosive, anarchic and swaggeringly rock ‘n’ roll, Ostermeier’s interpretation pushes past the play’s dissection of democratic debate and plunges us into a real, febrile one instead.
The whole thing has a contemporaneity that makes it feel urgent, a tribute both to Ibsen’s prescience and to Ostermeier’s rigorous analysis of its relevance.
But within it plays a satire that still retains some bite.
A fine, fluent cast, in particular Matt Smith, give a fast-moving, believable performance of a script whose humour assists the pacing without detracting too much from the seriousness of the issues.
Ostermeier's production is a bit too eager to be edgy in a midlife crisis sort of way.

This Enemy of the People courses with anger to burn, too much of it of the preemptive, predigested sort that pales into significance once you exit the theatre only to land back in the ongoing lacerations of life.
Nevertheless, it is a modern piece of live theatre that has to be seen, even if it does not quite live up to its billing and should be priced to be accessible to a wider youthful audience.
Ostermeier’s production smashes the fourth wall and gives us some revolutionary theatre.
It’s also hugely entertaining, funny, and expertly directed.

cn.t: Matt Smith electrifies in this audacious, fourth-wall-breaking Ibsen update, but critics divide sharply on whether Ostermeier's confrontational staging is urgently relevant or heavy-handed and arid.
